## Postulate

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ has absolute time $t$ in seconds and $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space with no distinguished origin. A Cartesian inertial chart is absolute time together with an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$, with spatial coordinates measured in metres. No relativistic causal structure is assumed. In this chart adopt a time-dependent orthonormal basis rotating uniformly about the chosen vertical unit vector $e_3=(0,0,1)$, with constant angular velocity vector $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega e_3$ in s$^{-1}$ and constant Coriolis parameter $f=2\Omega$ in this model's convention. The constant-$f$ choice is a local $f$-plane idealization; no latitude variation, planetary curvature, or $\beta$-plane term is included. The constant reference mass density $\rho_0>0$ has units kg m$^{-3}$; $f$ and $N$ have units s$^{-1}$; $g$ has units m s$^{-2}$; velocities have units m s$^{-1}$; and normalized pressure variables have units m$^2$ s$^{-2}$.

Adopt the following two distinct approximation branches; they are physical-model assumptions and not conclusions derived from mathematics.

1. **Linear, constant-stratification Boussinesq branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, use the flat periodic mathematical domain $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ with fundamental cell $Q_3=[0,2\pi]^3$, and represent fields by smooth $2\pi$-periodic lifts. Let $u:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be velocity, $b:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ a buoyancy-acceleration perturbation in m s$^{-2}$, and $\pi:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ pressure per reference density in m$^2$ s$^{-2}$; their displayed time and spatial derivatives are continuous, and $u,b$ have continuous second spatial derivatives. The positive constant reference density $\rho_0$ is used in inertia and the incompressibility constraint, while density-anomaly effects are retained only through the vertical buoyancy acceleration $b$. The buoyancy equation of state is not specified here. The Boussinesq approximation assumes fractional density anomalies small enough to neglect their effect on inertia while retaining their gravitational buoyancy effect. In addition, this branch adopts a linearization about a resting, uniformly stratified state: $N>0$ is a prescribed constant buoyancy-frequency parameter, and advection of the perturbations is omitted. For prescribed constants $f\in\mathbb R$ and $\nu,\kappa\ge 0$ in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, the model equations are

$$u_t+f e_3\times u+\nabla\pi=b e_3+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad b_t+N^2u_3=\kappa\Delta b.$$

Here $e_3\times u=(-u_2,u_1,0)$, $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\partial_{x_2}q,\partial_{x_3}q)$, $\nabla\cdot w=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}w_j$, and $\Delta q=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2q$, with $\Delta$ acting componentwise on $u$. The periodic domain is a mathematical boundary idealization. Neither this linear equation family nor the Boussinesq approximation includes a derived error estimate or asserts that a particular measured fluid satisfies the assumptions.

2. **One-layer shallow-water branch.** On the separate flat periodic domain $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$, let $h:I\times\mathbb T^2\to(0,\infty)$ be total layer depth in metres and $v:I\times\mathbb T^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be horizontal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, with the displayed derivatives continuous and second spatial derivatives continuous. Use constant $g>0$ in m s$^{-2}$ and constant $f\in\mathbb R$ in s$^{-1}$, and define $J(v_1,v_2)=(-v_2,v_1)$. Adopt a single layer with constant reference density, a flat bottom at vertical coordinate $z=0$, no bottom stress, no wetting or drying, and no interlayer coupling. Let $z$ be height positive upward in metres, $p(t,x_1,x_2,z)$ pressure in Pa, and $H,L>0$ representative vertical and horizontal length scales in metres. Assume the shallow-layer regime $H/L\ll1$; neglect vertical acceleration so pressure is hydrostatic, $\partial_zp=-\rho_0g$, with negligible pressure above the free surface $z=h(t,x_1,x_2)$, and take horizontal velocity independent of depth in the reduced model. The adopted hydrostatic profile is $p(t,x_1,x_2,z)=\rho_0g(h(t,x_1,x_2)-z)$ for $0\le z\le h(t,x_1,x_2)$. The resulting one-layer equations are

$$h_t+\nabla\cdot(hv)=0,\qquad (hv)_t+\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)+\nabla\!\left(\frac{g h^2}{2}\right)+f h Jv=0.$$

Here $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\partial_{x_2}q)$, $\nabla\cdot w=\partial_{x_1}w_1+\partial_{x_2}w_2$ for $w=(w_1,w_2)$, and tensor divergence is rowwise: $[\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)]_i=\sum_{j=1}^2\partial_{x_j}(h v_i v_j)$ for $i=1,2$.

The two-dimensional torus is again a mathematical boundary idealization, not a claim that a geophysical fluid occupies a torus. No reduction theorem or error estimate from the three-dimensional Boussinesq branch to this shallow-water branch is adopted. The branch assumptions specify when these equations are used as a model; they do not establish their empirical adequacy.

## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and use the periodic domain $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ with Lebesgue measure on $Q_3=[0,2\pi]^3$. Let $f\in\mathbb R$, $N>0$, and $\nu,\kappa\ge0$ be constants. Suppose $u,b$ are continuously differentiable in time and space with continuous second spatial derivatives, and $\pi$ has continuous first spatial derivatives; all fields are $2\pi$-periodic and satisfy

$$u_t+f e_3\times u+\nabla\pi=b e_3+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad b_t+N^2u_3=\kappa\Delta b.$$

Define the positive energy per reference density

$$E(t):=\frac12\int_{Q_3}\left(|u(t,x)|^2+\frac{b(t,x)^2}{N^2}\right)\,dx.$$

Then for every $t_0<t_1$ in $I$,

$$E(t_1)-E(t_0)=-\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\int_{Q_3}\left(\nu|\nabla u|^2+\frac{\kappa}{N^2}|\nabla b|^2\right)\,dx\,dt.$$

Thus the inviscid model conserves $E$, and the stated nonnegative diffusion coefficients make it nonincreasing. The condition $N>0$ is essential for this positive energy. This is an exact identity conditional on the displayed smooth linear Boussinesq equations; it is not a nonlinear or compressible stability theorem. A discrete analogue requires a skew Coriolis operator and compatible pressure/divergence pairing in the actual discretization; no claim is made for arbitrary schemes.

## Statement references

Equation family and pointwise regularity: [[def-fd-rotating-stratified-shallow-equations]].

Geoffrey K. Vallis, *Fluid Dynamics of the Atmosphere and Ocean*, §1.6.2–1.6.3, pp. 15–17: [full lecture notes, PDF](https://empslocal.ex.ac.uk/people/staff/gv219/ecmm719/lecnotes18w.pdf).

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is nonempty and open; $u,b,\pi$ are classical and $2\pi$-periodic in each spatial coordinate; $f\in\mathbb R$, $N>0$, and $\nu,\kappa\ge0$; the displayed equations hold pointwise.

[F1] [[def-fd-rotating-stratified-shallow-equations]]: the stratified branch on $\mathbb T^3$ is $u_t+f e_3\times u+\nabla\pi=b e_3+\nu\Delta u$, $\nabla\cdot u=0$, and $b_t+N^2u_3=\kappa\Delta b$, with constant $f\in\mathbb R$, $N>0$, and $\nu,\kappa\ge0$.

[F2] [[def-fd-rotating-stratified-shallow-equations]]: for a scalar field $q$, $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\partial_{x_2}q,\partial_{x_3}q)$; for a vector field $w$, $\nabla\cdot w=\sum_j\partial_{x_j}w_j$, $\Delta w$ is componentwise, $|w|^2=\sum_jw_j^2$, and $|\nabla w|^2=\sum_{i,j}(\partial_{x_j}w_i)^2$; $e_3\times w=(-w_2,w_1,0)$.

[A1] The fields satisfy these equations with the regularity in the statement, so every product and derivative below is continuous on each compact time interval times $Q_3$.

## Proof

1.1 Dot the momentum equation with $u$. Since $u\cdot(e_3\times u)=0$ pointwise and $u\cdot\nabla\pi=\nabla\cdot(\pi u)$ by the component definitions in [F2] and $\nabla\cdot u=0$, this gives $\partial_t(|u|^2/2)+\nabla\cdot(\pi u-\nu\sum_{i=1}^3u_i\nabla u_i)=bu_3-\nu|\nabla u|^2$. Here $u\cdot\Delta u=\nabla\cdot(\sum_i u_i\nabla u_i)-|\nabla u|^2$ follows by the product rule, component by component. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra]

2.1 Multiply the buoyancy equation by $b/N^2$ and use $b\Delta b=\nabla\cdot(b\nabla b)-|\nabla b|^2$ to get $\partial_t(b^2/(2N^2))+\nabla\cdot(-(\kappa/N^2)b\nabla b)=-bu_3-(\kappa/N^2)|\nabla b|^2$. Adding this to step 1.1 cancels the two $bu_3$ terms and yields a local energy balance with flux $\pi u-\nu\sum_i u_i\nabla u_i-(\kappa/N^2)b\nabla b$ and dissipation $\nu|\nabla u|^2+(\kappa/N^2)|\nabla b|^2$. [given, F1, F2, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Integrate the local balance over $Q_3\times[t_0,t_1]$. For each spatial coordinate, the integral of a periodic derivative over $[0,2\pi]$ is its endpoint difference and is zero; this removes the flux divergence. For each fixed $x$, the fundamental theorem of calculus converts the time derivative into the endpoint energy difference. Therefore the displayed integral identity holds. Since $N>0$, $E(t)\ge0$; since $\nu,\kappa\ge0$, the time-integrated dissipation is nonnegative. If $\nu=\kappa=0$, it vanishes identically and $E(t_1)=E(t_0)$. [given, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval. For $d=2,3$, define the flat periodic domain $\mathbb T^d:=\mathbb R^d/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^d$ and integrate over the fundamental cell $Q_d=[0,2\pi]^d$ using ordinary Lebesgue measure. A field on $\mathbb T^d$ is represented by its $2\pi$-periodic lift to the nonempty open spatial domain $\mathbb R^d$. All fields below are classical: their displayed time and spatial derivatives are continuous, and the velocity and buoyancy fields have continuous second spatial derivatives. Each displayed equation is a pointwise equality.

For a scalar field $q$, set $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\ldots,\partial_{x_d}q)$ and $\Delta q=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}^2q$. For a vector field $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_d)$, set $\nabla\cdot w=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}w_j$, $\Delta w=(\Delta w_1,\ldots,\Delta w_d)$, $|w|^2=\sum_{j=1}^dw_j^2$, and $|\nabla w|^2=\sum_{i,j=1}^d(\partial_{x_j}w_i)^2$. For a matrix field $A$, its divergence is rowwise: $(\nabla\cdot A)_i=\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_{x_j}A_{ij}$. In three dimensions $e_3\times u=(-u_2,u_1,0)$, and in two dimensions $Jv=(-v_2,v_1)$.

On $\mathbb T^3$, let $u:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be velocity, $b:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ be a buoyancy perturbation, and $\pi:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ be specific pressure. Let $e_3=(0,0,1)$, and prescribe constant parameters $f\in\mathbb R$, $N>0$, and $\nu,\kappa\ge0$. The rotating, linear, constant-stratification Boussinesq equation family is

$$u_t+f e_3\times u+\nabla\pi=b e_3+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad b_t+N^2u_3=\kappa\Delta b.$$

Here $\Delta$ acts componentwise, $u_3$ is the vertical velocity component, $f$ is the Coriolis coefficient, $N$ is the constant buoyancy-frequency parameter, and $\nu$ and $\kappa$ are the prescribed momentum and buoyancy diffusion coefficients. The inviscid branch is the choice $\nu=\kappa=0$. In the Boussinesq interpretation, a constant reference density is used in inertia and the divergence constraint while the density anomaly is retained through the vertical buoyancy force; small fractional density variation is an applicability assumption, not a theorem giving a compressible limit.

For its rotating-frame interpretation, take a time-dependent orthonormal Euclidean basis rotating uniformly about $e_3$ with constant angular velocity $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega e_3$, so $f=2\Omega$. The Coriolis acceleration on the force side is $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times u$, written on the left as $+f e_3\times u$. If $\Phi$ is gravitational potential per unit mass, define the effective potential by $\Phi_{\rm eff}(x):=\Phi(x)-\tfrac12|\boldsymbol\Omega\times x|^2$, which absorbs the centrifugal contribution. These frame and effective-potential choices are assumptions; the inertial-frame balance is distinct. The periodic domain is a mathematical idealization, not a claim that the physical fluid occupies a compact torus.

Independently, on $\mathbb T^2$, let $h:I\times\mathbb T^2\to(0,\infty)$ be total layer depth and $v:I\times\mathbb T^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be horizontal velocity. Let $g>0$ and $f\in\mathbb R$ be prescribed constants, define $Jv:=(-v_2,v_1)$, and take a fixed flat bottom. The inviscid one-layer shallow-water equation family is

$$h_t+\nabla\cdot(hv)=0,\qquad (hv)_t+\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)+\nabla\!\left(\frac{g h^2}{2}\right)+f h Jv=0.$$

The tensor divergence is rowwise, $(\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v))_i=\sum_{j=1}^2\partial_{x_j}(h v_i v_j)$. This family has one layer, positive depth, a flat bottom, and no bottom friction, wetting/drying, or interlayer coupling. These are mathematical equation systems, not assertions that a measured fluid realizes them. With SI interpretation, $t$ is in seconds, spatial coordinates in metres, $u$ and $v$ in metres per second, $b$ in metres per second squared, $\pi$, $\Phi$, and $\Phi_{\rm eff}$ in square metres per square second, $f$, $N$, and $\Omega$ in inverse seconds, $\nu$ and $\kappa$ in square metres per second, $h$ in metres, and $g$ in metres per square second. thm-fd-shallow-water-smooth-energy:
## Statement

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and use $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ with Lebesgue measure on $Q_2=[0,2\pi]^2$. $$h_t+\nabla\cdot(hv)=0,\qquad (hv)_t+\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)+\nabla\!\left(\frac{g h^2}{2}\right)+f h Jv=0,$$

## Postulate

Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds and $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space with no distinguished origin. Choose a Cartesian inertial chart with an orientation-preserving affine isometry $X:E\to\mathbb R^3$, in metres, and the absolute-time coordinate. Its coordinate origin is a fixed inertial point; no relativistic causal structure is assumed. Fix $t_r\in I$ and a constant $\Omega\in\mathbb R$ in s$^{-1}$, set $\theta(t)=\Omega(t-t_r)$, and define

$$R(t)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta(t)&-\sin\theta(t)&0\\\sin\theta(t)&\cos\theta(t)&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad x(t,q)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}X(q)\quad(q\in E).$$

The map $(t,q)\mapsto(t,x(t,q))$ is the adapted rotating Cartesian chart, a rigid observer change in the stated frame convention. Its orthonormal basis vectors have inertial components $R(t)e_i$, where $e_i$ are the standard coordinate unit vectors; the basis is associated with the chart, rather than itself being called a frame. For a $C^2$ worldline $q(t)$ with inertial-coordinate velocity $V(t)=dX(q(t))/dt$, its rotating-coordinate velocity is

$$\frac{dx}{dt}=R(t)^{\mathsf T}V(t)-\Omega e_3\times x(t,q(t)),\qquad e_3=(0,0,1).$$

Thus $u$ below denotes velocity relative to the rotating chart, not merely rotated components of $V$; the shallow-water $v$ denotes the first two components of this relative velocity in its separate depth-independent reduced model. The rotation is right-handed about $e_3$, with angular-velocity vector $\boldsymbol\Omega=\Omega e_3$ and Coriolis parameter $f=2\Omega$. In this convention the modeled Coriolis acceleration is $-2\boldsymbol\Omega\times u$ on the force side, hence $+f e_3\times u$ on the left of the momentum equation. Constant rotation has no angular-acceleration term. Centrifugal acceleration is incorporated into the prescribed background effective potential: if $\Phi$ is gravitational potential per unit mass in rotating coordinates, its effective value is $\Phi_{\rm eff}(t,x)=\Phi(t,x)-|\boldsymbol\Omega\times x|^2/2$. The local constant effective gravity and resting background pressure are adopted before the perturbation equations below; $\pi$ is the perturbation pressure per reference density. These are adopted local approximations and linearization choices, not an exact Newtonian coordinate-transformation derivation of the displayed reduced systems. Periodicity below is imposed on the perturbation fields in rotating coordinates; it does not require that $R(t)$ map a fixed periodic lattice to itself or that the background potential be periodic.

Adopt the following two distinct approximation branches; they are physical-model assumptions and not conclusions derived from mathematics.

1. **Linear, constant-stratification Boussinesq branch.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval, use the flat periodic mathematical domain $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb R^3/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ with fundamental cell $Q_3=[0,2\pi]^3$, and represent fields by $2\pi$-periodic lifts with the regularity specified next. Let $u:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be velocity, $b:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ a buoyancy-acceleration perturbation in m s$^{-2}$, and $\pi:I\times\mathbb T^3\to\mathbb R$ pressure per reference density in m$^2$ s$^{-2}$; $u,b$ have continuous first time and spatial derivatives and continuous second spatial derivatives, and $\pi$ has continuous first spatial derivatives. The positive constant reference density $\rho_0$ is used in inertia and the incompressibility constraint, while density-anomaly effects are retained only through the vertical buoyancy acceleration $b$. The buoyancy equation of state is not specified here. The Boussinesq approximation assumes fractional density anomalies small enough to neglect their effect on inertia while retaining their gravitational buoyancy effect. In addition, this branch adopts a linearization about a resting, uniformly stratified state: $N>0$ is a prescribed constant buoyancy-frequency parameter, and advection of the perturbations is omitted. For prescribed constants $f\in\mathbb R$ and $\nu,\kappa\ge 0$ in m$^2$ s$^{-1}$, the model equations are

$$u_t+f e_3\times u+\nabla\pi=b e_3+\nu\Delta u,\qquad \nabla\cdot u=0,\qquad b_t+N^2u_3=\kappa\Delta b.$$

Here $e_3\times u=(-u_2,u_1,0)$, $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\partial_{x_2}q,\partial_{x_3}q)$, $\nabla\cdot w=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}w_j$, and $\Delta q=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2q$, with $\Delta$ acting componentwise on $u$. The periodic domain is a mathematical boundary idealization. Neither this linear equation family nor the Boussinesq approximation includes a derived error estimate or asserts that a particular measured fluid satisfies the assumptions.

2. **One-layer shallow-water branch.** On the separate flat periodic domain $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$, let $h:I\times\mathbb T^2\to(0,\infty)$ be total layer depth in metres and $v:I\times\mathbb T^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be horizontal velocity in m s$^{-1}$, with continuous first time and spatial derivatives and continuous second spatial derivatives. Use constant $g>0$ in m s$^{-2}$ and constant $f\in\mathbb R$ in s$^{-1}$, and define $J(v_1,v_2)=(-v_2,v_1)$. Adopt a single layer with constant reference density, a flat bottom at vertical coordinate $z=0$, no bottom stress, no wetting or drying, and no interlayer coupling. Let $z$ be height positive upward in metres, $p(t,x_1,x_2,z)$ pressure in Pa, and $H,L>0$ representative vertical and horizontal length scales in metres. Assume the shallow-layer regime $H/L\ll1$; neglect vertical acceleration so pressure is hydrostatic, $\partial_zp=-\rho_0g$, with negligible pressure above the free surface $z=h(t,x_1,x_2)$, and take horizontal velocity independent of depth in the reduced model. The adopted hydrostatic profile is $p(t,x_1,x_2,z)=\rho_0g(h(t,x_1,x_2)-z)$ for $0\le z\le h(t,x_1,x_2)$. The resulting one-layer equations are

$$h_t+\nabla\cdot(hv)=0,\qquad (hv)_t+\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)+\nabla\!\left(\frac{g h^2}{2}\right)+f h Jv=0.$$

Here $\nabla q=(\partial_{x_1}q,\partial_{x_2}q)$, $\nabla\cdot w=\partial_{x_1}w_1+\partial_{x_2}w_2$ for $w=(w_1,w_2)$, and tensor divergence is rowwise: $[\nabla\cdot(hv\otimes v)]_i=\sum_{j=1}^2\partial_{x_j}(h v_i v_j)$ for $i=1,2$.

The two-dimensional torus is again a mathematical boundary idealization, not a claim that a geophysical fluid occupies a torus. No reduction theorem or error estimate from the three-dimensional Boussinesq branch to this shallow-water branch is adopted. The branch assumptions specify when these equations are used as a model; they do not establish their empirical adequacy.
